quests.definition: 'Cut in' means to interrupt someone while they're talking, often rudely, before they finish their point. It can also describe a car pulling suddenly into a lane in front of you.
quests.exampleSentence: She kept cutting IN every time I tried to explain my idea.
quests.example: She kept cutting IN every time I tried to explain my idea.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'CUT' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal in the driving sense, and figurative in conversation — you're not literally cutting anything, just breaking into someone's speech.
quests.nativeTip: This means interrupting someone while they're speaking.

quests.definition: 'Drag on' means for something, like a meeting, a speech, or a story, to continue for longer than expected in a tedious or boring way.
quests.exampleSentence: The meeting dragged ON for nearly three hours, with no clear decision made.
quests.example: The meeting dragged ON for nearly three hours, with no clear decision made.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'DRAG' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally being pulled — the phrase compares a slow, tedious event to something being dragged forward with effort.
quests.nativeTip: This describes something, like a meeting or a movie, feeling too long and boring.

quests.definition: 'Sum up' means to briefly state the main points of something, usually at the end of a discussion, presentation, or piece of writing. It's a natural way to signal that you're about to conclude.
quests.exampleSentence: To sum UP, we're on track for the deadline but still need more testing.
quests.example: To sum UP, we're on track for the deadline but still need more testing.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'SUM' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is added together — the phrase compares condensing information into a short conclusion to totaling numbers.
quests.nativeTip: This means briefly stating the main points of something at the end.

quests.definition: 'Bottle up' means to hide or suppress your feelings instead of expressing them, often until they build up to an unhealthy level. It suggests emotions are being sealed away rather than released.
quests.exampleSentence: He tends to bottle UP his frustration instead of talking about it.
quests.example: He tends to bottle UP his frustration instead of talking about it.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'BOTTLE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally placed in a bottle — the phrase compares suppressed emotion to something contained and sealed shut.
quests.nativeTip: This means hiding your feelings instead of expressing them.

quests.definition: 'Burst into' (tears, laughter, song) means to suddenly begin doing something intensely and without warning, especially crying or laughing. The suddenness and intensity are the key parts of the meaning.
quests.exampleSentence: She burst INTO tears the moment she heard the good news.
quests.example: She burst INTO tears the moment she heard the good news.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'INTO' combines with the verb 'BURST' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically bursts — the phrase captures the sudden, forceful start of an emotional reaction.
quests.nativeTip: This means suddenly starting to cry or laugh without warning.

quests.definition: 'Lash out' means to react suddenly and angrily, sometimes verbally and sometimes physically, often at someone who isn't really the cause of the frustration.
quests.exampleSentence: He lashed OUT at his teammate after missing the final shot, even though it wasn't really his fault.
quests.example: He lashed OUT at his teammate after missing the final shot, even though it wasn't really his fault.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'LASH' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally struck with a whip — the phrase compares an angry outburst to a sudden, forceful lashing motion.
quests.nativeTip: This means reacting to something with sudden anger, often unfairly toward someone nearby.

quests.definition: 'Keep up (with)' means to maintain the same pace as others, or to stay current with something that changes quickly, like news or technology. It's different from 'keep on,' which is about continuing an action rather than matching a pace.
quests.exampleSentence: The industry changes so fast that it's hard to keep UP with all the new tools.
quests.example: The industry changes so fast that it's hard to keep UP with all the new tools.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'KEEP' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically kept in place — the phrase compares matching someone's pace or staying informed to not falling behind physically.
quests.nativeTip: This means maintaining the same pace as others, or staying current with something changing quickly.

quests.definition: 'Catch on' can mean for something, like a trend or a new product, to become popular. It can also mean to understand something, a different sense you'll encounter again later, so context always decides which meaning applies.
quests.exampleSentence: The new app didn't catch ON right away, but within a year everyone was using it.
quests.example: The new app didn't catch ON right away, but within a year everyone was using it.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'CATCH' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally caught — the phrase compares an idea spreading in popularity to catching hold and taking off.
quests.nativeTip: This means an idea, trend, or product suddenly becoming popular.

quests.definition: 'Build up' means for something to increase gradually over time, such as pressure, excitement, experience, or even traffic. It emphasizes a slow accumulation rather than a sudden change.
quests.exampleSentence: Tension had been building UP between the two departments for months before the argument.
quests.example: Tension had been building UP between the two departments for months before the argument.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'BUILD' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Works literally for physical accumulation, like sediment building up, and figuratively for things like stress or anticipation increasing.
quests.nativeTip: This describes something, like pressure or excitement, increasing gradually over time.

quests.definition: 'Splash out (on something)' means to spend a generous, sometimes extravagant amount of money on something special, rather than being cautious with your budget.
quests.exampleSentence: For their anniversary, they splashed OUT on a fancy dinner and a night at a hotel.
quests.example: For their anniversary, they splashed OUT on a fancy dinner and a night at a hotel.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'SPLASH' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no liquid is involved — the phrase compares generous spending to splashing water around freely and without restraint.
quests.nativeTip: This means spending a generous, sometimes extravagant, amount of money.

quests.definition: 'Shell out (for something)' means to pay for something, often reluctantly, especially when the amount feels like more than you wanted to spend.
quests.exampleSentence: We had to shell OUT nearly two hundred dollars to fix the car's brakes.
quests.example: We had to shell OUT nearly two hundred dollars to fix the car's brakes.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'SHELL' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally shelled — the phrase compares reluctantly parting with money to cracking open a shell to get at what's inside.
quests.nativeTip: This means paying for something, often reluctantly, because it's expensive or unwanted.

quests.definition: 'Set aside' means to save or reserve something — money, time, or resources — for a specific purpose later. It's often used for savings, but also for putting a task or feeling aside temporarily.
quests.exampleSentence: We try to set ASIDE a little money every month for emergencies.
quests.example: We try to set ASIDE a little money every month for emergencies.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ASIDE' combines with the verb 'SET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative for money and time — nothing is physically moved to the side — though it borrows the image of placing something out of the main flow to keep for later.
quests.nativeTip: This means saving or reserving something, like money or time, for a specific future use.

quests.definition: 'Back out (of something)' means to withdraw from an agreement, deal, or commitment you had already made, often at the last moment. This is a third distinct meaning of 'back,' different from copying data or supporting someone, taught earlier.
quests.exampleSentence: He agreed to be our best man but backed OUT two weeks before the wedding.
quests.example: He agreed to be our best man but backed OUT two weeks before the wedding.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'BACK' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no physical backward movement occurs — the phrase compares withdrawing from a commitment to stepping backward away from it.
quests.nativeTip: This means withdrawing from an agreement or promise you had already made.

quests.definition: 'Sign off (on something)' means to give final, formal approval, often used for documents, budgets, or projects that need official confirmation before moving forward.
quests.exampleSentence: The design looks great, but we still need the client to sign OFF on it.
quests.example: The design looks great, but we still need the client to sign OFF on it.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'SIGN' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Mostly figurative — you may or may not literally sign a document — but the phrase always implies giving official, final approval.
quests.nativeTip: This means formally giving final approval to something, such as a document or plan.

quests.definition: 'Follow through (on something)' means to complete an action you started or promised, rather than abandoning it partway. It's often used to describe reliability, or the lack of it.
quests.exampleSentence: It's easy to make plans, but it's harder to follow THROUGH on them.
quests.example: It's easy to make plans, but it's harder to follow THROUGH on them.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'THROUGH' combines with the verb 'FOLLOW' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically passes through anything — the phrase describes carrying a commitment all the way to completion.
quests.nativeTip: This means completing an action you already started or promised to do.

quests.definition: 'Show off' means to display your abilities, possessions, or achievements in a way meant to impress others, often seen as boastful or excessive.
quests.exampleSentence: He can't resist showing OFF his new car to anyone who will listen.
quests.example: He can't resist showing OFF his new car to anyone who will listen.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'SHOW' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally displayed on a shelf — the phrase describes drawing attention to yourself in a boastful way.
quests.nativeTip: This means behaving in a way meant to impress or draw attention to your abilities.

quests.definition: 'Look down on someone' means to regard them as inferior, less important, or less worthy of respect. It's the opposite attitude of respecting someone as an equal.
quests.exampleSentence: She never looks DOWN ON people just because they have less money than her.
quests.example: She never looks DOWN ON people just because they have less money than her.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'DOWN ON' combines with the verb 'LOOK' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one is physically looking downward at another person — the phrase compares feeling superior to someone to literally looking down from above.
quests.nativeTip: This means regarding someone as inferior or less important than yourself.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ LOOK + DOWN ON ➔ LOOK DOWN ON

quests.definition: 'Stand up for someone' means to defend or support them, especially when they're being criticized, bullied, or treated unfairly. Together with 'stand up' (rise physically) and 'stand by' (remain loyal), this completes a small family of 'stand' phrases with related but distinct meanings.
quests.exampleSentence: She always stands UP FOR her younger brother when other kids tease him.
quests.example: She always stands UP FOR her younger brother when other kids tease him.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP FOR' combines with the verb 'STAND' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one physically rises to defend another person — the phrase compares taking someone's side to physically standing beside them.
quests.nativeTip: This means defending or supporting someone, especially when they're being criticized or treated unfairly.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ STAND + UP FOR ➔ STAND UP FOR

quests.definition: 'Speak out (against something)' means to publicly express a strong opinion, especially in opposition to something unfair or wrong. It's stronger and more public than 'speak up,' which can simply mean talking a little louder.
quests.exampleSentence: Several employees spoke OUT against the company's new policy.
quests.example: Several employees spoke OUT against the company's new policy.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'SPEAK' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically moves outward — the phrase emphasizes making an opinion public and known, especially in protest.
quests.nativeTip: This means publicly expressing a strong opinion, often against something unfair.

quests.definition: 'Call out' means to publicly identify and criticize someone for behavior considered wrong or unacceptable. This is a third meaning of 'call,' different from 'call back' (return a call) and 'call off' (cancel), taught earlier.
quests.exampleSentence: A customer called the company OUT online for its misleading advertising.
quests.example: A customer called the company OUT online for its misleading advertising.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'CALL' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one is literally calling from a distance — the phrase describes publicly drawing attention to someone's wrongdoing.
quests.nativeTip: This means publicly criticizing someone for behavior you think is wrong.

quests.definition: 'Side with someone' means to support their position in an argument or disagreement, rather than staying neutral or supporting the other party.
quests.exampleSentence: In most family arguments, their grandmother sided WITH whoever seemed most upset.
quests.example: In most family arguments, their grandmother sided WITH whoever seemed most upset.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'WITH' combines with the verb 'SIDE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: no one physically moves to a side — the phrase describes aligning your opinion or support with one party in a dispute.
quests.nativeTip: This means supporting one person or group in an argument or dispute.

quests.definition: 'Come up' means for something unexpected to happen or arise, often disrupting existing plans, such as a sudden problem or opportunity. It's a very common way to explain a last-minute change.
quests.exampleSentence: I'm sorry to cancel, but something urgent came UP at work.
quests.example: I'm sorry to cancel, but something urgent came UP at work.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'COME' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically rises — the phrase compares an unexpected event appearing to something surfacing suddenly.
quests.nativeTip: This means something unexpected has happened or arisen, often disrupting a plan.

quests.definition: 'Come round (to something)' means to eventually accept or agree with an idea you initially opposed. It can also mean to regain consciousness after fainting — two very different situations sharing the same phrase.
quests.exampleSentence: He was against the idea at first, but he eventually came ROUND to it after seeing the results.
quests.example: He was against the idea at first, but he eventually came ROUND to it after seeing the results.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ROUND' combines with the verb 'COME' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative for changing an opinion, and closer to literal for regaining consciousness, since your awareness genuinely 'comes back' after fainting.
quests.nativeTip: This means gradually accepting an idea you initially disliked, or regaining consciousness.

quests.definition: 'Come off' can mean for a plan or attempt to succeed, as in 'the surprise party came off perfectly,' or, literally, for something attached to become detached, like a button coming off a shirt. Together with 'come up' and 'come round,' this rounds out a family of meanings from one simple verb.
quests.exampleSentence: Considering how complicated the plan was, it's amazing it came OFF so smoothly.
quests.example: Considering how complicated the plan was, it's amazing it came OFF so smoothly.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'COME' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Works figuratively for a plan succeeding, and literally for an object detaching — context always signals which sense is intended.
quests.nativeTip: This can mean a plan working out successfully, or an object becoming loose and detaching.

quests.definition: 'Live up to (something)' means to be as good as expectations, a reputation, or a standard suggested. It's often used when discussing whether something meets the high hopes people had for it.
quests.exampleSentence: The sequel didn't quite live UP TO the excitement of the first film.
quests.example: The sequel didn't quite live UP TO the excitement of the first film.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP TO' combines with the verb 'LIVE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing physically rises to meet anything — the phrase compares meeting expectations to reaching a level others hoped you would.
quests.nativeTip: This means being as good as people expected you to be.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ LIVE + UP TO ➔ LIVE UP TO

quests.definition: 'Measure up (to something)' means to be as good as required by a particular standard, closely related to 'live up to' but often used when directly comparing to a specific benchmark or competitor.
quests.exampleSentence: The new hire's work simply didn't measure UP to what the role required.
quests.example: The new hire's work simply didn't measure UP to what the role required.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'MEASURE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is literally measured with a ruler — the phrase compares meeting a standard to matching a required size or length.
quests.nativeTip: This means being good enough compared to a particular standard.

quests.definition: 'Fall short (of something)' means to fail to reach a required standard, target, or expectation. It completes a wide family of 'fall' meanings you've now studied — fall out, fall behind, fall apart, fall through, and now fall short.
quests.exampleSentence: Ticket sales fell SHORT of what the organizers had hoped for.
quests.example: Ticket sales fell SHORT of what the organizers had hoped for.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'SHORT' combines with the verb 'FALL' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nobody physically falls — the phrase compares failing to reach a goal to landing before reaching the intended distance.
quests.nativeTip: This means failing to meet a standard, expectation, or target.

quests.conceptTitle: Phrasal Anatomy: WRAP wrap it up
quests.definition: This revisits the separable-verb pattern with 'wrap up,' meaning to finish something. With a noun you can say 'wrap up the meeting' or 'wrap the meeting up,' but with a pronoun like 'it,' the particle must follow the pronoun: 'wrap it up.'
quests.exampleSentence: The presentation has run long, so let's wrap it up and take questions later.
quests.example: The presentation has run long, so let's wrap it up and take questions later.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'wrap it up' combines with the verb 'WRAP' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This question is about grammar, not a new meaning — 'wrap up' still means to finish; only the pronoun's position changes.
quests.nativeTip: This reviews 'wrap up' from earlier in this file — remember how pronouns affect word order in separable phrasal verbs.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ WRAP + wrap it up ➔ WRAP wrap it up

quests.definition: This revisits 'catch on' with its other common meaning: to understand or grasp something, often after a period of confusion, rather than the 'become popular' sense taught earlier in this file. The same two words can point to a trend or to a person's understanding.
quests.exampleSentence: It took him a while, but he finally caught ON to what the joke meant.
quests.example: It took him a while, but he finally caught ON to what the joke meant.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'CATCH' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Figurative: nothing is physically caught — the phrase compares finally understanding something to catching hold of an idea that had been slipping away.
quests.nativeTip: This means finally understanding something, often after some initial confusion.

quests.conceptTitle: Phrasal Anatomy: GET THE HANG OF
quests.definition: 'Get the hang of (something)' means to learn how to do something and become comfortable with it, usually after some initial practice or difficulty. It's a fitting phrase to close this stage of your learning — a reminder that fluency with phrasal verbs themselves comes the same way, with steady practice.
quests.exampleSentence: It took a few tries, but she finally got THE HANG OF using chopsticks.
quests.example: It took a few tries, but she finally got THE HANG OF using chopsticks.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'THE HANG OF' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Fully figurative: nothing is literally hanging — the phrase describes reaching a comfortable, practiced understanding of a new skill.
quests.nativeTip: This means becoming familiar and skilled with something new through practice.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ GET + THE HANG OF ➔ GET THE HANG OF
